title: SVP hardness for fixed-rank cyclotomic modules
formal:
Does exact Euclidean shortest-vector decision remain NP-hard on cyclotomic module lattices when the module rank is an absolute constant?

For each fixed integer \(r\ge1\), let \(\mathcal D_r\) be the decision problem defined below. A valid instance consists of a conductor \(m\ge3\), finitely many generators \(y_1,\ldots,y_s\in R_m^r\) spanning \(K_m^r\) over \(K_m\), and an integer squared threshold \(S\ge0\), where
\[K_m=\mathbb Q(\zeta_m),\quad R_m=\mathbb Z[\zeta_m],\quad M=\sum_{j=1}^s R_m y_j.\]
It is a YES instance exactly when \(\lambda_1(M)^2\le S\), using the canonical product norm below.

The target is the existence of a fixed \(r\), a deterministic multitape Turing machine \(F\), and positive integer constants \(C,d\) such that \(F\) runs in at most \(C(N+1)^d\) bit steps on every input string of length \(N\), and for every well-formed 3-CNF formula \(\varphi\), it outputs a valid instance of \(\mathcal D_r\) satisfying
\[\varphi\text{ is satisfiable}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\lambda_1(M_{F(\varphi)})^2\le S_{F(\varphi)}.\]
Thus one rank and one uniform polynomial-time many-one reduction must work for all formulas; the conductor, generators and threshold may depend on the formula.
why: Module lattices retain algebraic structure while permitting much larger families than single ideals. Establishing hardness with a fixed number of module coordinates would show that this compact structure can support a fundamental worst-case geometric obstruction as the field degree grows. The problem tests the boundary between algebraic organization and computational difficulty; exact worst-case hardness alone does not establish the security of cryptographic parameter distributions.
status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. Bennett’s 2023 source poses the constant-rank hardness question. Liu–Feng–Pan arXiv:2609.01469v1, submitted 1 September 2026, now claims a matching positive answer for a prime-conductor cyclotomic rank-two subfamily under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions. The theorem’s norm, rank, representation and exact decision threshold were checked against this explicit variant. Its full proof was not independently certified, so the card remains uncertain rather than being archived as a verified resolution. The result does not assert the separate power-of-two, rank-one or average-case cryptographic statements.

sentences: Cyclotomic module lattices combine integer lattice geometry with multiplication by an algebraic number ring.
The question asks whether exact Euclidean shortest-vector decision is NP-hard at some fixed module rank while the conductor and field degree grow.
The card specifies the canonical product norm, integral generators and a uniform deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction.
A September 2026 preprint claims this hardness already for rank two over a prime-conductor subfamily, matching the selected formulation.
The complete new proof is independently unverified here, and its claim does not imply hardness for every ring family or cryptographic distribution.

definitions:
For an integer \(m\ge3\), let \(\zeta_m=\exp(2\pi i/m)\). The degree \(n=\phi(m)\) is the number of integers \(a\) with \(1\le a\le m\) and \(\gcd(a,m)=1\). Define the monic cyclotomic polynomial
\[\Phi_m(X)=\prod_{\substack{1\le a\le m\\\gcd(a,m)=1}}(X-\zeta_m^a)\in\mathbb Z[X].\]
The ring \(R_m\) is identified with \(\mathbb Z[X]/(\Phi_m(X))\); it is the full ring of integers in \(K_m\). Every ring element is written uniquely by its \(n\) integer coefficients in the basis \(1,\zeta_m,\ldots,\zeta_m^{n-1}\).

A module generated by \(y_1,\ldots,y_s\) is the set of all sums \(\sum_j a_jy_j\) with \(a_j\in R_m\). Here \(s\ge r\) is finite and may vary. The input promise is that the columns have rank \(r\) over the field \(K_m\). Hence the generated additive group has integer rank \(rn\) and is a full lattice in the real span of its canonical embedding. The ring rank \(r\) stays fixed, while the integer dimension \(rn\) can grow. Generators may be redundant; the module is not promised free over \(R_m\) or principal in rank one. Integral coordinates are required, with no supplied factorization or pseudo-basis oracle.

For \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_r)\in K_m^r\), the canonical product norm is
\[\|x\|_{\mathrm{can}}^2=\sum_{i=1}^r\sum_{\substack{1\le a\le m\\\gcd(a,m)=1}}|\sigma_a(x_i)|^2,\qquad\sigma_a(\zeta_m)=\zeta_m^a.\]
Equivalently it is \(\sum_i\operatorname{Tr}_{K_m/\mathbb Q}(x_i\overline{x_i})\), where conjugation sends \(\zeta_m\) to \(\zeta_m^{-1}\). All embeddings, including both members of each conjugate pair, are included. The real lattice dimension is \(rn\), despite representing it with complex coordinates. Set \(\lambda_1(M)=\min\{\|x\|_{\mathrm{can}}:x\in M\setminus\{0\}\}\). Discreteness and full rank make this a positive attained minimum. Squared norms of integral module vectors are integers. The comparison includes equality at the threshold and requires no approximation or gap promise. A threshold of zero gives a valid NO instance.

To specify the bit model, encode each nonnegative integer \(a\) as \(U(a)=1^\ell0b\), where \(b\) is its binary expansion without leading zeros and \(\ell=|b|\); zero uses \(b=0\). Encode signed integers by one sign bit and \(U\) of the absolute value, using the positive sign for zero. A module input writes \(U(m),U(s),U(S)\), then all \(rsn\) signed coefficients, ordered by generator, module coordinate and power-basis coefficient. All coefficients, including zeros, are explicitly present. The fixed \(r\) is a parameter of the language, not part of the input. Invalid encodings, conductors less than three and rank-deficient lists are rejected in \(\mathcal D_r\). The reduction must produce valid inputs on both satisfiable and unsatisfiable well-formed formulas.

A 3-CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses with exactly three signed variable occurrences each; repetitions are allowed. Use an encoding consisting of a unary number of declared variables, a binary length-delimited clause count, and three sign/index pairs for each clause, with every index in the declared variable range. The empty conjunction is satisfiable. All clauses and occurrences are written explicitly. Malformed formula strings need not have a correctness guarantee for \(F\), but the global polynomial clock still applies.

The reduction uses one finite classical program and a fixed finite number of tapes. Each step has the usual bounded-symbol read/write and one-cell head movement cost. Arithmetic, construction of the conductor and ring data, and every written output bit are charged. No randomness, quantum computation, advice, hard-instance table depending on input length or uncharged oracle is allowed. The output length is bounded by the same polynomial clock. The chosen rank and constants are independent of formula size. The statement asks for hardness at at least one fixed rank over the specified family, not at every rank or at a fixed conductor. This exact decision language is a yes/no target; it is not a request to estimate a shortest length numerically.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated existence or its full negation. A positive answer must supply a fixed rank, a uniform deterministic reduction and universal polynomial clock, and prove validity and the YES–NO equivalence for every well-formed formula. A negative answer must rule out such a reduction for every fixed rank, rather than refute a proposed construction or fail to establish hardness at one rank. A randomized reduction, a Turing reduction making several oracle queries, growing module rank, hardness for a non-Euclidean norm, or a security assumption about random keys does not establish this specified claim. It is not necessary to prove \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) in order to prove a reduction.

source_formulation.text: Bennett’s Open Problem 4.9 asks for NP-hardness at some constant module rank over some family of base rings, with power-of-two cyclotomics given as an example. The example is not a mandatory restriction. This card makes the cyclotomic-family variant precise by allowing all conductors, choosing the canonical Euclidean product embedding, integral finite generator lists, exact squared thresholds and deterministic many-one reductions. It retains the existential fixed-rank quantifier, rather than requiring rank two, rank one or hardness for every fixed rank. The family/embedding choice is an explicit editorial specification of the source’s choices. Hardness on the prime-conductor rank-two subfamily would answer this variant affirmatively; it would not establish the separate power-of-two or rank-one questions.

context_blocks.text: A fixed module rank is compatible with an unbounded geometric dimension: rank \(r\) over a degree-\(n\) number field gives integer dimension \(rn\). The hard-instance family must therefore vary the underlying field as inputs grow. Treating “rank two” as a two-dimensional integer lattice would erase the central distinction in the question.

Rank-one modules include ideals, whereas higher rank permits interactions between several ring coordinates. Bennett presents the fixed-rank module question after the ideal-lattice hardness question as a broader target. The distinction between module rank and the number of listed generators also matters: redundant generators do not increase the rank over the field.

The original survey distinguishes exact decision SVP from approximate decision and search variants. Its use of GapSVP does not itself require an approximation gap: factor one is the exact threshold decision problem. The card therefore uses an exact squared threshold and asks for a deterministic reduction, with the norm and representation fixed explicitly.

Felderhoff, Pellet-Mary and Stehlé relate a promised module unique-SVP problem to NTRU and give a random self-reduction with an ideal-SVP oracle qualification. Those are reductions between structured lattice problems with an exceptional-short-vector promise. The checked abstract does not claim a deterministic reduction from an NP-complete problem to the exact decision language in this card.

De Boer, Page, Toma and Wesolowski’s 2025 preprint, presented at STOC 2026, gives a worst-case-to-average-case self-reduction for approximate SIVP at fixed module rank. Its abstract specifies the Extended Riemann Hypothesis, a discretized invariant distribution, and a polynomial loss in approximation. SIVP seeks independent short vectors; a self-reduction of that task does not establish NP-hardness of exact SVP.

Liu, Feng and Pan’s 1 September 2026 preprint claims NP-completeness of exact decision SVP for full-rank free modules of rank two over \(\mathbb Z[\zeta_q]\), where the conductor \(q\) ranges over primes congruent to three modulo four. Theorem 1.1 specifies deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, integral generators, a nonzero determinant and an integer squared threshold under the canonical product norm. These instances belong to the card’s family with \(r=2\).

If that claim is correct, it answers the selected existential-rank question affirmatively even with two generators. Its Corollary 1.2 separately states search hardness under Turing reductions. The paper explicitly excludes conclusions about a fixed cyclotomic ring, the power-of-two family, average-case hardness or a cryptographic security reduction. The theorem and model were matched here, but the complete new proof was not independently certified; the card is therefore uncertain.

The earlier ideal-SVP algorithmic advances give an additional reason to distinguish rank one from rank two. Cramer, Ducas and Wesolowski’s cyclotomic ideal result is quantum, has a \(\exp(\widetilde O(\sqrt m))\) approximation scale, and has stated number-theoretic hypotheses for its polynomial-time consequence. It is neither an exact decision algorithm for all fixed-rank modules nor a contradiction to an exact hardness claim.
